# On the Strange Comfort of Uncertainty

I've been thinking about how we treat certainty like a currency we're desperate to hoard, when maybe it's actually less valuable than we think.

There's this peculiar comfort in not knowing. A friend told me recently that she loved the middle of a good book—not the beginning (you're still orienting) or the ending (you're just waiting to see if you were right), but that fat middle where anything could still happen. Where the character could still choose differently, still surprise you.

I think we live most of our lives in the ending, though. We rush toward conclusions: about people, about what things mean, about what we're capable of. We collect certainties like they're going out of style, as if arriving at a fixed opinion about something is the same as understanding it.

But certainty is sort of the opposite of attention. When you're certain about something, you stop looking at it. You stop noticing the ways it contradicts itself, evolves, surprises you.

The smartest people I know tend to be comfortable with a kind of permanent bewilderment. Not confused exactly—they understand plenty—but fundamentally uncertain about the larger questions. How to live. What matters. Who they are. They don't seem to suffer from this. If anything, they seem freer.

Maybe the goal isn't to figure it all out, but to get better at being lost.
